newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-PIENAAR SETS SIGHTS ON ENGLAND CAP.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-PIENAAR SETS SIGHTS ON ENGLAND CAP.

text.p: When Nelson Mandela handed the Webb Ellis trophy to Springbok captain Francois Pienaar after South Africa had beaten New Zealand in the 1995 Rugby World Cup final, it symbolised the birth of a new nation.
Here was the first black African President of the new republic in total harmony and communion with the old oppressor, the blond Afrikaner, so much so he even wore Pienaar's number six jersey.

It is strange to think, then, that three years from now Mandela, who has stated his intention not to serve another term, will no longer be President and Pienaar, who captained the Springboks in all 29 of his tests, could be wearing not the green and gold of South Africa but the lilywhite of England.

Pienaar, 30, has played only one club match since signing a two-match contract with London side Saracens last month, but has said he is keen to make himself eligible for England by satisfying the 36-month residency clause under International Board regulations.
"Jack Rowell (England coach) has got a great number of players here to choose from but if I do get picked then I would definitely be available. Definitely," said Pienaar.
"I would love to play for South Africa first of all. That is my country, I love the passion in the game in South Africa, and the game has done a lot for me so, yes, South Africa is my priority.
"But at the moment, with the current coach, that doesn't look likely. I know I can still compete at that level and I want to play international rugby.

"If my play in three years is up to the required standard and if the restrictions are lifted then I am not going to say no to England, I wouldn't think twice about it. And I'll play as hard as I can."
Pienaar's fall from grace last year, just 12 months after winning the World Cup, provided one of the more surprising chapters in South African sport.
The key lay in a change of coach when Andre Markgraaff took over from World Cup-winning boss Kitch Christie who was forced to stand down because of illness.

Pienaar was in the team for the start of the Tri-Nations series against New Zealand and Australia but once he had been concussed against the All Blacks at Newlands, Markgraaff decided he was surplus to requirements.

"When I was concussed we were 18-6 ahead and when I woke up we had lost the test which was a bit of a surprise for me," says Pienaar. "Perhaps I was dropped for being injured, maybe they thought I got concussed too much."
His omission from the squad to tour Argentina, France and Wales was met with disbelief at home. One of the selectors, Ray Mordt, resigned and Markgraaff received a tirade of hate-mail.
Pienaar laughs about it now but admits he was shocked at the time.

"I was very heartsore at that point. But you quickly realise that everyone gets dropped down the line, you just have to accept it whatever the reasons. And there were plenty of those. I realised I wasn't wanted."

The Springboks, led by Gary Teichmann, had a successful tour winning all five of their tests which left Pienaar, who only turned 30 at the start of January, with the choice of staying in South Africa to play provincial rugby for Transvaal, or perhaps Western Province, or teaming up with Saracens.
Encouraged by his wife of a year, he chose the latter and signed a two-year contract.

"There are no bigger things to achieve in South Africa. How much bigger does it get...the most famous person in the world being overjoyed and wearing my jersey? I think I experienced something that I don't think anyone else will experience in their lives. For that I will always be grateful.
"But this is a new adventure for me and I have a lot of goals here in England." Including, perhaps, an England cap.
